results.name: digit_reversal_target_contrast
results.description: Yes rate for non-member targets whose digits are the reverse of some example (e.g. 72 after 27, two-digit, non-palindromic), minus the yes rate for all other non-member targets in the same sets; observed above null means people generalise to digit reversals more than the model (which has no digit-order concepts) predicts.
results.code:
# name: digit_reversal_target_contrast
# description: Yes rate for non-member targets whose digits are the reverse of some example (e.g. 72 after 27, two-digit, non-palindromic), minus the yes rate for all other non-member targets in the same sets; observed above null means people generalise to digit reversals more than the model (which has no digit-order concepts) predicts.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy().astype(float)
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    k = np.sum(~np.isnan(ex), axis=1)
    lo = np.nanmin(ex, axis=1)
    hi = np.nanmax(ex, axis=1)
    member = np.any(ex == t[:, None], axis=1)
    exr = np.where(np.isnan(ex) | (ex < 10) | (ex > 99) | (ex % 11 == 0), np.nan, (ex % 10) * 10 + ex // 10)
    rev = np.any(exr == t[:, None], axis=1) & ~member
    has = np.any(~np.isnan(exr) & (exr >= 10), axis=1)
    a = rev; b = has & ~rev & ~member
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())

results.name: even_inspan_targets_all_odd_sets
results.description: Yes rate for even targets strictly inside the span of sets whose 3-4 examples are all odd; observed above null means the model's odd-number rule suppresses in-range generalisation more than people do (people treat such sets as ranges).
results.code:
# name: even_inspan_targets_all_odd_sets
# description: Yes rate for even targets strictly inside the span of sets whose 3-4 examples are all odd; observed above null means the model's odd-number rule suppresses in-range generalisation more than people do (people treat such sets as ranges).
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy().astype(float)
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    k = np.sum(~np.isnan(ex), axis=1)
    lo = np.nanmin(ex, axis=1)
    hi = np.nanmax(ex, axis=1)
    member = np.any(ex == t[:, None], axis=1)
    allodd = np.all(np.isnan(ex) | (ex % 2 == 1), axis=1)
    sel = (k >= 3) & allodd & (t % 2 == 0) & (t > lo) & (t < hi)
    if sel.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[sel].mean())

results.name: single_example_above_minus_below
results.description: For one-example sets, yes rate for targets above the example minus yes rate for targets below it (target != example); observed above null means people generalise upward more than the model's symmetric range prior predicts, below means downward more.
results.code:
# name: single_example_above_minus_below
# description: For one-example sets, yes rate for targets above the example minus yes rate for targets below it (target != example); observed above null means people generalise upward more than the model's symmetric range prior predicts, below means downward more.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy().astype(float)
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    k = np.sum(~np.isnan(ex), axis=1)
    lo = np.nanmin(ex, axis=1)
    hi = np.nanmax(ex, axis=1)
    member = np.any(ex == t[:, None], axis=1)

results.name: round_target_just_outside_contrast
results.description: Among non-member targets 1-10 outside the example span of multi-example sets, yes rate for multiples of 10 minus yes rate for other targets; observed above null means people extend ranges to round numbers more than the round-edge prior predicts, below means less.
results.code:
# name: round_target_just_outside_contrast
# description: Among non-member targets 1-10 outside the example span of multi-example sets, yes rate for multiples of 10 minus yes rate for other targets; observed above null means people extend ranges to round numbers more than the round-edge prior predicts, below means less.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy().astype(float)
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    k = np.sum(~np.isnan(ex), axis=1)
    lo = np.nanmin(ex, axis=1)
    hi = np.nanmax(ex, axis=1)
    member = np.any(ex == t[:, None], axis=1)
    d = np.where(t > hi, t - hi, np.where(t < lo, lo - t, 0))
    sel = (k >= 2) & (d >= 1) & (d <= 10) & ~member
    rnd = (t % 10 == 0)
    a = sel & rnd; b = sel & ~rnd
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())

results.name: decade_crossing_outside_contrast
results.description: Among non-member targets 1-9 outside the span of multi-example sets, yes rate for targets in the same decade (same tens digit, 100 counted with 90s) as the nearest edge example minus yes rate for targets in a different decade; observed above null means people treat decades as category boundaries more than the model predicts, below means less.
results.code:
# name: decade_crossing_outside_contrast
# description: Among non-member targets 1-9 outside the span of multi-example sets, yes rate for targets in the same decade (same tens digit, 100 counted with 90s) as the nearest edge example minus yes rate for targets in a different decade; observed above null means people treat decades as category boundaries more than the model predicts, below means less.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy().astype(float)
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    k = np.sum(~np.isnan(ex), axis=1)
    lo = np.nanmin(ex, axis=1)
    hi = np.nanmax(ex, axis=1)
    member = np.any(ex == t[:, None], axis=1)
    d = np.where(t > hi, t - hi, np.where(t < lo, lo - t, 0))
    edge = np.where(t > hi, hi, lo)
    dec = lambda x: np.minimum((x - 1) // 10, 9)
    sel = (k >= 2) & (d >= 1) & (d <= 9) & ~member
    same = dec(t) == dec(edge)
    a = sel & same; b = sel & ~same
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())

results.name: weber_outside_generalisation_contrast
results.description: Yes rate for non-member targets 1-15 outside the span of sets lying entirely at or above 50, minus the same rate for sets lying entirely at or below 35; observed above null means people generalise further (in absolute distance) for large numbers than the model's magnitude-independent ranges allow (Weber-like scaling), below means the reverse.
results.code:
# name: weber_outside_generalisation_contrast
# description: Yes rate for non-member targets 1-15 outside the span of sets lying entirely at or above 50, minus the same rate for sets lying entirely at or below 35; observed above null means people generalise further (in absolute distance) for large numbers than the model's magnitude-independent ranges allow (Weber-like scaling), below means the reverse.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy().astype(float)
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    k = np.sum(~np.isnan(ex), axis=1)
    lo = np.nanmin(ex, axis=1)
    hi = np.nanmax(ex, axis=1)
    member = np.any(ex == t[:, None], axis=1)
    d = np.where(t > hi, t - hi, np.where(t < lo, lo - t, 0))
    near = (d >= 1) & (d <= 15) & ~member
    a = near & (lo >= 50); b = near & (hi <= 35)
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())

results.name: odd_inspan_targets_all_even_sets
results.description: Yes rate for odd targets strictly inside the span of sets of 2+ all-even examples that do not all share a last digit; observed below null means people apply an even-number rule more strictly than the model (model over-generalises the range to odd numbers), above means less strictly.
results.code:
# name: odd_inspan_targets_all_even_sets
# description: Yes rate for odd targets strictly inside the span of sets of 2+ all-even examples that do not all share a last digit; observed below null means people apply an even-number rule more strictly than the model (model over-generalises the range to odd numbers), above means less strictly.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy().astype(float)
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    k = np.sum(~np.isnan(ex), axis=1)
    lo = np.nanmin(ex, axis=1)
    hi = np.nanmax(ex, axis=1)
    member = np.any(ex == t[:, None], axis=1)
    alleven = np.all(np.isnan(ex) | (ex % 2 == 0), axis=1)
    last = np.where(np.isnan(ex), np.nan, ex % 10)
    samelast = np.nanmax(last, axis=1) == np.nanmin(last, axis=1)
    sel = (k >= 2) & alleven & ~samelast & (t % 2 == 1) & (t > lo) & (t < hi)
    if sel.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[sel].mean())
